title: How many times is a town bigger than a school?
description: To compare a town with a school, both areas must be in the same unit. The school ground is changed to square metres, the town is changed from square kilometres to square metres, and the bigger area is divided by the smaller one. The numbers in the video are an example, and the child uses the numbers of their own school and town.
teaching_notes: One idea: write both areas in the same unit, then divide the bigger by the smaller. Watch for students who divide square kilometres by square metres without changing a unit.

source: How many times is your village, town or city bigger than your school
video_script.why: The child has met the square kilometre and knows it holds one million square metres, and now compares a big area with a small one.
video_script.substitution: The book question has no numbers because it uses the child's own school and town. The school ground of one hundred metres by eighty metres and the town of ten square kilometres are an example chosen here.
video_script.anchor: a school ground of one hundred metres by eighty metres beside a town of ten square kilometres, as an example
video_script.payoff_line: In this example the town is one thousand two hundred fifty times as big as the school ground.

final_answer.value: 1250 times for a 10 km² town and an 8000 m² school
final_answer.spoken: one thousand two hundred fifty times for a town of ten square kilometres and a school of eight thousand square metres

maths_rules: check by rounding 8000 up to 10000: 10000000 / 10000 = 1000; 8000 is less than 10000, so the answer is more than 1000
the child must use their own school and town data in the same steps
video_script.design: A small school ground and a big town stay on the board with example sizes written beside them. The working changes both to square metres and then divides. The video says clearly that the numbers are an example and the child uses their own.
open_questions: The book gives no numbers because the question uses the child's own school and town, so the sizes in this video are an example from the worklist.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; a school ground 100 m by 80 m beside a much bigger town marked 10 km²; the word example is written above them

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.school: the school ground appears with its sides 100 m and 80 m
marks.town: the much bigger town appears marked 10 km²
marks.ask: a question mark appears between them

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about your school and your town.
<bookmark mark='school'/>Suppose the school ground is one hundred metres by eighty metres.
<bookmark mark='town'/>Suppose the town covers ten square kilometres.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How many times is the town bigger than the school?

beats.on_screen: the school and the town stay on the board and Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: m² and km² are written side by side with 1 km² = 1000000 m²; the town is shown in m²

marks.same: the units m² and km² are written side by side
marks.change: 1 km² = 1000000 m² is written between them

narration: <bookmark mark='same'/>We use the same way as the example in your book. Both areas must be in the same unit before we compare them.
<bookmark mark='change'/>A square kilometre is huge and a square metre is small. One square kilometre is one million square metres.

beats.on_screen: Given (example): school ground 100 m by 80 m; town 10 km²

marks.school: the school ground sides are written

narration: <bookmark mark='school'/>Given, the ground is one hundred metres by eighty metres.
<bookmark mark='town'/>The town is ten square kilometres. These are example numbers, so use your own school and town.

beats.on_screen: To find: how many times the town is bigger than the school

marks.find: the words how many times bigger are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find how many times the town is bigger than the school.

marks.rule: the rule length × breadth, 100 × 80, is written
marks.val: 8000 m² is written inside the ground

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step one, find the school ground. Its area is length times breadth, one hundred times eighty.
<bookmark mark='val'/>That gives eight thousand square metres.

marks.rule: 10 × 1000000 is written because each km² is 1000000 m²
marks.val: 10000000 m² is written inside the town

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step two, change the town to square metres. Each square kilometre is one million square metres, so multiply ten by one million.
<bookmark mark='val'/>That gives ten million square metres.

marks.fit: school grounds of 8000 m² are laid one after another inside the town of 10000000 m²

narration: <bookmark mark='fit'/>Step three, we find how many school grounds fit in the town.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Divide ten million by eight thousand.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check by rounding 8000 up to 10000: 10000000 ÷ 10000 = 1000, and 8000 is less than 10000, so the answer is more than 1000
narration: <bookmark mark='round'/>Step four, check by rounding eight thousand up to ten thousand.
<bookmark mark='est'/>Ten million divided by ten thousand is one thousand. Eight thousand is less than ten thousand. The answer must be more than one thousand.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 10000000 ÷ 8000 = 1250; in this example the town is 1250 times as big as the school ground

marks.own: the words use your own school and town are written under the box

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>In this example the town is one thousand two hundred fifty times as big as the school ground.
<bookmark mark='own'/>That is more than one thousand, as the check said. For your own town and school, use your own numbers in the same steps.
